cards.title: The Rule of One: Anchor Each Ad and Landing Page to a Single Big Idea
cards.summary: Michael Masterson's Rule of One says compelling sales messages center on one big idea rather than stacked selling points, with evidence from 91 of the top 100 offers.
cards.use_when: Deciding the core message for a paid social ad, landing page, advertorial, or PDP before briefing creative or writing copy.
steps: Before writing, select one big idea to be the 'tip of the spear' for the ad or page. Everything else is subordinate to it.
Apply Masterson's three tests to the candidate idea: it must be easy to understand, easy to believe, and interesting or unique. If it fails any test, keep hunting.
Strip out competing selling points. Masterson calls stacked, unrelated claims 'tossed salad copy' — throwing many selling points in hoping one sticks, which dilutes conversion power.

Make all sub-bullets, arguments, facts, and stories serve only to reinforce the single concept. A 'six morning strategies' list works only if all six are sub-points of one core benefit; if each is unrelated, it is a tossed salad.
Review your best-converting ads and check whether they share simplicity, directness, and clarity — use them as evidence for how narrow your message should be.
Recognize the hard part is choosing the one idea, not writing the copy. The writing gets simpler once the single idea is fixed.
caveats: The 91-of-100 claim comes from Masterson's review of top historical offers and is the source's evidence, not a guaranteed outcome at your scale.
The presenter's opinion that the best-converting ads are 'the ones that do best are the simplest' is a personal observation, not a universal rule.

cards.title: Audit Ad and Page Copy for 'Tossed Salad' Clutter
cards.summary: Diagnose cluttered messaging that stacks unrelated selling points, then consolidate it into one reinforcing argument.
cards.use_when: Reviewing an underperforming ad, landing page, or advertorial that has accumulated multiple selling points over iterations.
steps: Read the creative or page and list every distinct selling point, claim, and benefit that appears.
Flag any point that is not a sub-point of the same core idea — those are the tossed-salad elements.
Identify which single point is easiest to understand, easiest to believe, and most unique. That becomes the candidate big idea.
Rewrite remaining sub-bullets, stories, facts, and arguments so each one reinforces that one concept rather than introducing a new angle.
If a strong sub-point cannot be made to reinforce the core idea, cut it; do not keep it 'just in case'.
Re-read the final message and check that a stranger could state its one argument back in a sentence.
caveats: Cutting compelling-but-off-topic points is uncomfortable; the source frames that discomfort as the forcing function that improves selection.
This is a messaging framework, not a testing protocol — validate any rewrite with your own ad or page tests.

cards.title: Use the Rule of One to Force a Single USP
cards.summary: A USP should be one core proposition everyone immediately understands, not nineteen competing propositions.
cards.use_when: Defining or revising the unique selling proposition for a product launch, brand campaign, or product page.
steps: Gather every plausible selling proposition you have for the product or offer.
Apply Masterson's three criteria as a filter: easy to understand, easy to believe, counterintuitive or unique.
Select one proposition as the anchor. The source is explicit that you want one core selling proposition, not 19.
Position that proposition as the central claim of the ad, landing page, and any supporting advertorial.
Check that the proposition is believable — a counterintuitive claim that is not credible will not move buyers.
Use the selected USP to decide which supporting proof, testimonials, and facts belong on the page, and which to drop.
caveats: The source presents this as Masterson's framework rather than a tested rule; results depend on product and audience.
Uniqueness that isn't believable fails the framework's own test — don't chase novelty alone.

10-MCR / paid social creative and content

Goes here. Paid social creative production, hook writing, direct response video frameworks, creator/UGC scripting, static ad design, messaging strategies, evaluating stages of awareness, identifying new ad formats/angles, advertorials, unique mechanisms, and creative strategist workflows.

Not here.

Paid advertising performance metrics, ROAS, scaling rules, bidding, or ad-platform specific attribution -> 11-ADC

Conversion rate optimization (CRO) on core website pages or general analytics -> 06-MEA

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details Michael Masterson's "Rule of One" copywriting framework from Great Leads, emphasizing that high-converting sales messages and advertisements must focus on a single, compelling big idea that is easy to understand, believable, and unique rather than relying on "tossed salad copy." modules: [MCR] topics: [creative strategy, messaging and positioning] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. creative strategy / Applying the "Rule of One" framework to ad copy and creative messaging. Avoiding cluttered "tossed salad copy" (stacking multiple unrelated selling points) in favor of focusing an advertisement or landing page around one single, centralized big idea. Ensuring all sub-bullets, arguments, and supporting stories serve exclusively to reinforce that core message, acting as the tip of the spear for consumer acquisition. messaging and positioning / Structuring marketing messages so they are easy to understand, easy to believe, and uniquely interesting. Using the single big idea to anchor the Unique Selling Proposition (USP), forcing marketers to ruthlessly select the most powerful angle rather than confusing the marketplace with fragmented value propositions.

Look for. The definition of "tossed salad copy": throwing multiple different selling points into an advertisement or message hoping something sticks, which dilutes conversion power. The core principle of the "Rule of One": 91% of top-performing historical offers center on a single, unified big idea. The three elements of a successful single big idea: it must be easy to understand, easy to believe, and unique/interesting.

Skip. General social media outro remarks (e.g., "like and subscribe").

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume. 10 to 15.
